title: Seven Days to the DeployCo Interview
description: The coding test is not LeetCode, there is no AI environment, and Python fundamentals are what they say they want. Here is the seven day plan built around those constraints.

lines.text: You have seven days. The coding test has no AI environment.
It is not LeetCode. It is Python fundamentals in a practical build.
So just grind LeetCode for a week and you will be fine.
No, because that trains the wrong muscle entirely.
LeetCode teaches you to spot a trick in a puzzle. DeployCo wants to see if you can build a thing that works under real constraints.
Then what do I actually practise?
That is exactly what this episode answers.
Here is the stake. This role pays up to three hundred and sixty thousand Australian dollars plus equity.
That is a serious number for a role that is essentially consulting with code.
It is not consulting. Forward deployed engineers embed with clients, understand the domain, and ship production systems.
Colin Jarvis, who runs the practice, says the job of an FDE is to eat pain and excrete product.
Charming image. But it tells me they value shipping over theorising.
Exactly. And your seven days should reflect that.
This is The DeployCo Screen. Today we plan your seven days.
The recruiter confirmed three things about the coding test.
First, no AI tools allowed. You write every line yourself.
Second, it focuses on Python fundamentals, not algorithmic puzzles.
Third, it is not LeetCode style. It is a practical build task.
Every recruiter says fundamentals matter. That is boilerplate.
In this case it is not boilerplate, because the task style proves it.
Candidates report building rate limiters with sliding windows, key value stores with expiry, credit management systems with audit trails.
Those sound like things you would actually build on the job.
Because that is the point. They are testing whether you can ship working code, not whether you memorised a solution.
There is also a system design component covering LLM deployment architecture, eval driven development, retrieval design, cost and latency tradeoffs.
So the decision is not what to study but how to spend each day?
Exactly. Seven days, each with a specific target and a specific deliverable.
Three ideas to hold onto all week.
First, eval driven development.
Colin Jarvis built OpenAI's forward deployed team from scratch in twenty twenty two.
He says code is not done until evals verify efficacy. Not until it compiles. Not until it looks right. Until evals prove it works.
That sounds like something you put on a slide to impress investors.
Except it has direct consequences for how they grade take homes.
Your own project was graded partly on whether the eval assertions actually checked correctness or just checked that results existed.
A membership check says did we get anything back. A constraint check says are these results actually correct for the query.
And they can tell the difference from reading the code?
Absolutely. If your test says assert length is greater than zero, that tells them nothing about quality.
Second idea: determinism over language models wherever possible.
Jarvis showed a supply chain demo where deterministic guardrails verify every model output before the user sees it.
If a rule engine can answer it, use a rule engine. Reserve the model for natural language understanding.
Is that not obvious?
It is obvious in hindsight. But most people reach for the model first because it feels like the modern answer.
Third idea: do what does not scale. Their team watchword.
Wait, is not scaling badly a bad thing?
Not early. Jarvis says the biggest mistake teams make is generalising a solution before understanding the problem.
Ship something scrappy for one client. Learn. Then generalise if the pattern holds.

sources.title: Colin Jarvis on Forward Deployed Engineering at OpenAI

lines.text: Let us walk through all seven days beat by beat.
Day one, today, is a diagnostic. Build a sliding window rate limiter in sixty minutes.
Thread safe, memory bounded, no AI assistance.
At exactly minute thirty, a new requirement arrives. Burst support and a remaining count instead of a boolean.
Why inject a requirement change mid-task? That seems designed to stress people out.
Because that is literally the job. At a client site, requirements change while you are mid-sprint.
They want to see if you refactor gracefully or freeze up.
Day two, three coding drills back to back.
Drill one: key value store with expiry and thread safety. Forty five minutes.
Drill two: refactor deliberately ugly nested code into clean composable pieces. Thirty minutes.
Drill three: credit management system with spending, refunds, and an audit trail. Forty five minutes.
That is two hours of coding in one day.
Yes, and that is intentional. You need stamina as much as skill.
Day three morning: rebuild the key value store but write every single test before writing any implementation.
This forces you to think about what correct means before you start coding.
Day three afternoon: a staged grid simulation. Agents move, collisions detected, walls block paths.
New requirements injected at thirty and sixty minutes, same pattern as day one.
Day four: system design using an eight step framework.
Clarify who the user is and what failure costs. Map the data flow. Design evals. Model the cost. Budget latency.
Decide which parts are deterministic versus LLM. Address failure modes. Then ask what breaks at ten times traffic.
The exercise is designing a fintech customer support chatbot. Ten thousand concurrent users, p ninety nine under three seconds, five hundred dollars monthly budget.
Day five: defend your existing project. Know its weaknesses specifically, not vaguely.
Your grader said prose outran code. Be ready to explain what that means and how you fixed it.
Should you bring up weaknesses unprompted?
Only when asked. But know the answers cold so there is no hesitation.
Day six: full dress rehearsal. Brand new coding task and a fresh system design scenario.
Same rules. No AI. Timed. Requirement injection at the halfway mark.
And day seven? Please say rest.
Light review only, one hour maximum. A tired expert loses to a rested intermediate every time.

lines.text: Now the numbers that decide this interview.
Sixty minutes for the live coding test. Not ninety. Not thirty.
If the task has three components, that gives you roughly twenty minutes per component.
Subtract ten minutes for setup, imports, and reading the spec carefully. You have fifty minutes of actual coding time.
That is tight for someone who is used to having AI autocomplete.
Which is why you practise without it starting today. Muscle memory matters here.
Your existing project scored twenty three out of thirty from an independent grader.
Production thinking scored three out of five. Communication scored four out of five.
What specifically cost those points?
Documentation promised things the code did not do. Decision table drift. A docstring promising price filtering that was not implemented.
Same failure mode in three places. Writing better than verifying.
The salary range is one hundred and thirty five thousand to three hundred and sixty thousand Australian dollars plus equity.
That range spans junior to principal level. They calibrate the interview to find your level within it.
So a junior candidate gets a simpler task than a principal?
Probably the same base task but higher expectations on edge cases and testing rigour for senior candidates.
The requirement change comes at exactly minute thirty. Halfway through.
If you are still writing your first function at minute forty, the interview is already lost.
DeployCo launched in May twenty twenty six with four billion dollars in investment and a pre money valuation of ten billion dollars.
They acquired Tomoro, which had about one hundred and fifty forward deployed engineers.
Arnaud Fournier is chief technology officer. He co-founded OpenAI's FDE team and was the first forward deployed engineer ever hired.
So the person making hiring decisions invented the role you are interviewing for?
Effectively yes. Which means he knows exactly what good looks like and cannot be bluffed.

lines.text: Three ways this preparation week goes sideways.
First, grinding LeetCode because it feels productive and everyone else does it.
LeetCode teaches you binary search on a rotated sorted array. DeployCo asks you to implement a thread safe queue with retry logic.
Different skills entirely. One is puzzle solving. The other is engineering.
But LeetCode is what everyone else prepares with. Does it not help at least a little?
Marginally, for basic syntax fluency. But the marginal hour spent on a practical drill is worth ten hours of LeetCode for this specific interview.
Second way it goes wrong: spending all seven days on system design and neglecting live coding fluency.
System design is important but the coding test is the gate. You must pass it to reach the design conversation.
If you fail live coding, nobody hears your beautiful architecture diagram.
Third way: over preparing your project defence until every answer sounds scripted.
There is a difference between rehearsed and prepared.
What is the difference exactly?
Rehearsed means every answer is polished, none of them admit uncertainty, and it sounds like you are reading from notes.
Prepared means you know your weaknesses specifically, you can talk about them without defensiveness, and you have thought about what you learned.
The early signal that you are over rehearsed: if your practise answers never change between takes, they are too rigid.
One more failure mode: neglecting sleep in the final forty eight hours.
Everyone says that though.
Everyone says it and nobody believes it until they walk into an interview having slept four hours and cannot remember how to initialise a lock.
Three questions to ask yourself each morning this week.
Can I build a practical Python system in under forty five minutes without any AI assistance?
Not theoretically. Actually timed, with a stopwatch running.
Can I explain why I chose deterministic code instead of a language model for a given step in my design?
If your answer is because it seemed better, that is not enough. You need a reason grounded in cost, latency, or correctness.
Do I know what broke in my last significant project, and can I describe it without getting defensive?
Not what went wrong in theory. What actually broke, what was the root cause, and what do you do differently now?
One question to test yourself right now.
If someone asked you to implement a thread safe counter with a time to live expiry, could you start writing code immediately?
Not after thinking about it. Immediately. Lock placement, data structure choice, expiry check on read.
If yes, you are ready for Day Two. If no, start with the drills tonight.
What about the system design side? Are you walking through that next?
That is the next episode. We design a fintech chatbot end to end using the eight step framework.
Every number estimated, every failure mode addressed, and the determinism choices justified.
I will hold you to the budget constraint.
Good. Because that is exactly what DeployCo will do too.
